title: A Steady Gaze on a Solid Object

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 80: Looking without a story (Y56 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: sthūlarūpasya bhāvasya stabdhāṃ dṛṣṭiṃ nipātya ca | acireṇa nirādhāraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā śivaṃ vrajet ||
dharana.rendering: Having let a steady, unmoving gaze fall on some solid, physical thing, and soon making the mind free of support, one goes to Śiva.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: fix the gaze without blinking on a gross object while directing attention inward; 'without support' means free of thought-constructs, which are the mind's props. Singh identifies this as the bhairavī mudrā and classes it as śāmbhavopāya. Wallis: 'making the mind free of thoughts and projections about that being'.

instruction: Rest a steady gaze on one simple object and let go of all thoughts about it.

method.text: Place a simple object in front of you. Let the gaze rest on it steadily. Let go of names, judgments and stories about it, so the mind has nothing to lean on. Blink whenever the eyes need to.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 80 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: One simple object, seen steadily
attention.secondary: The mind letting go of thoughts about it

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a straight line of gaze from the eyes to one simple object, with the mind letting go of everything it thinks about that object.
points: a simple physical object (a stone, a cup, a candle-holder)

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Blink whenever needed: the classical gaze is unblinking, but this school does not ask for it. Stop if the eyes water or strain. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Mouth Open, Mentally Sounding 'Ha'

dharana.sanskrit_iast: madhyajihve sphāritāsye madhye nikṣipya cetanām | hoccāraṃ manasā kurvaṃs tataḥ śānte pralīyate ||
dharana.rendering: With the mouth wide open and the tongue in the middle, placing awareness in the middle, and sounding 'ha' in the mind, one dissolves into peace.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh reads the tongue as inverted against the palate (khecarī mudrā, as described in the Vivekamārtaṇḍa) and explains: the breath naturally sounds haṃsa; with the tongue inverted the 's' cannot form and only 'ha' remains, a vowel-less 'ha' that can only be sounded mentally, and repeating it develops the middle state. Wallis and Bäumer read 'the tongue in the middle of the wide open mouth'; Wallis adds 'pointing up'. This door follows the plain reading and does not teach tongue inversion.

instruction: Let the mouth fall open, rest the tongue in the middle, and silently sound 'ha'.

method.text: Let the jaw relax so the mouth opens wide, without strain. Rest the tongue in the middle of the mouth. Place awareness in the middle of that open space and sound 'ha' silently, in the mind only. Let it dissolve into peace.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 81 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath through the nose or the open mouth, whichever is comfortable. The 'ha' is silent, in the mind only. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The middle of the open mouth
attention.secondary: The silent, mental 'ha'

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the open space of the mouth, the tongue resting in its middle, and a silent 'ha' sounding in that space.
points: the tongue resting in the middle
the mental sound 'ha' in the middle of the open space

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Open the mouth only as wide as is comfortable; close it whenever the jaw tires. Tongue inversion is not taught. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: The Body Contemplated as Unsupported

dharana.sanskrit_iast: āsane śayane sthitvā nirādhāraṃ vibhāvayan | svadehaṃ manasi kṣīṇe kṣaṇāt kṣīṇāśayo bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: Resting on a seat or a bed, let one contemplate one's own body as without support; as the mind fades, in an instant one becomes free of one's stored dispositions.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: though actually resting on a seat or bed, one contemplates with firm conviction that the body has no support at all; the mind becomes free of the thought-constructs that serve as its props, and with that the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) lying in the unconscious also vanish. Wallis: 'floating without support'.

instruction: Resting on a seat or bed, feel your body as if nothing were holding it up.

method.text: Sit on a seat or lie on a bed, fully supported. Then contemplate the body as having no support at all, as if floating in open space. Let the mind quieten as it loses its props.

title: When a Sense Is Blocked, the Void Behind It

dharana.rendering: When any sense, whichever it is, is obstructed (by something striking it from outside) or deliberately blocked, one enters the non-dual void, and right there the Self shines.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: when a sense is obstructed by an external cause, naturally, or by a self-imposed device, it cannot contact the world, a feeling of emptiness arises in it, the mind turns inward and is absorbed in a void without subject-object duality, where the Self is revealed. Bäumer reads vyāghāta as obstruction 'by striking (an external object)'.

instruction: Gently block one sense, such as covering the ears, and rest in the empty space that opens.

method.text: Gently block one sense: rest the palms lightly over the ears, or use earplugs, or simply close the eyes. Notice the emptiness that appears where the sense was reaching out, and rest in that space. Also notice such moments when they happen by themselves, such as a sudden silence.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 89 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The empty space that appears when one sense is gently blocked
attention.secondary: The Self shining there

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is one sense going quiet, and the empty, inward space that appears where it used to reach outward.
points: the gentle block (palms over the ears)
the empty space where the sense had been reaching out

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Use only gentle blocks: palms resting lightly on the ears, earplugs, or closed eyes. Never press on the eyes or ears, and never block the nose or mouth. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Sounding the Plain Letter 'A'

dharana.sanskrit_iast: abindum avisargaṃ ca akāraṃ japato mahān | udeti devi sahasā jñānaughaḥ parameśvaraḥ ||
dharana.rendering: For one who repeats the letter 'a' without the nasal dot (bindu) and without the out-breathed 'ḥ' (visarga), O Goddess, a great flood of knowledge, the Supreme Lord, rises suddenly.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: 'a' with bindu would be 'aṃ' (an in-breath) and with visarga 'aḥ' (an out-breath); without either, it implies sounding 'a' in a state of breath retention, according to the commentary. Lakshmanjoo instead reads the commentary's 'retention' as a posture of the mouth (cakita mudrā: mouth wide open, tongue drawn back), so that 'a' can only be sounded mentally. 'A' is chosen as the first letter, source of all others, the symbol of the absolute (anuttara) and of perfect I-consciousness (aham).

instruction: Repeat a soft, plain 'a' sound, aloud or silently, with no hum and no breathy ending.

method.text: Sound a soft, plain 'a' (as in 'father'), without closing it into a hum and without letting it end in a breathy 'h'. Repeat it gently, aloud or in the mind. Rest in the open quality of the sound.

title: At the End of the Out-Breathed 'Ḥ'

dharana.rendering: Place awareness at the end of the visarga of a syllable that carries a visarga (the out-breathed 'ḥ'); with a mind free of support, one touches the eternal brahman.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.

Fixing the mind at the very end of that sound, the symbol of manifestation, the mind is detached from manifestation and slips into the void, steeped in the silence of brahman.

instruction: Softly sound 'aḥ' and rest attention at the exact point where the breathy 'ḥ' fades into silence.

title: Stillness at the Heart of a Strong Emotion

title: A Supportless Mind That Builds No Thoughts
sanskrit: nirādhāraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā vikalpān na vikalpayet

numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 108 'Dharana 85', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 84. Not followed.

dharana.sanskrit_iast: nirādhāraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā vikalpān na vikalpayet | tadātmaparamātmatve bhairavo mṛgalocane ||
dharana.rendering: Making the mind supportless, let one not construct thought-constructs; then, O doe-eyed one, in the self becoming the supreme self, there is Bhairava.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: 'all supports' means external supports, such as perceiving objects, and internal ones, such as imagination, concepts, pleasure and pain; one should be rid of thought-constructs (vikalpa). The constructing mind is the empirical self; the non-constructing awareness is the spiritual Self, witness of all states. Singh classes it as śāmbhavopāya. Wallis: 'don't fabricate'.

instruction: Let the mind rest on nothing, and do not build on any thought that appears.

method.text: Let the mind rest on nothing: no object, no image, no idea. When a thought appears, do not build on it; let it pass. Rest in the open awareness that remains.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 108 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The mind leaning on no support, outer or inner
attention.secondary: Not assembling thoughts; letting any that come pass

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a mind leaning on nothing, outer or inner, and not building anything new.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If this becomes effortful, rest attention lightly on the breath for a while. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

honesty.disclosure: Door 084 follows Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 84 (verse 108) in Jaideva Singh's numbering. The door-to-dharana index is a School of 112 Doorways teaching device. Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.
